title: The color in the line
intro:
It is 35 minutes into the first shift on a Tuesday. Mr. Ramon Santos, 59, dialyzes through a right arm fistula. He tells the nurse, Ms. Grace Villar, that his back and upper abdomen hurt and he feels like vomiting. His blood pressure is usually around 140/80 mm Hg. Today it reads 178/98.

Twelve patients are on machines. The technician changed the carbon tanks yesterday afternoon. Ms. Villar calls you over.

n1.prompt: What do you look at first, after airway, breathing, and circulation?

choices.text: The blood in his venous line, the needle sites, and the circuit.
choices.feedback: Back and abdominal pain with a rising pressure on dialysis is a pattern to respect. Looking at the blood in the line takes seconds and can show translucent, port-wine colored blood: hemolysis.
choices.then: The blood in the venous line is bright and see-through, like red wine held to the light. The needles are secure. There is no kink in the lines.

choices.text: An ECG, because back pain and a fast pulse could be the heart.
choices.feedback: An ECG is reasonable and he will need a monitor. But the color of the blood in the line is the faster clue here, and it changes what you do in the next minute.
choices.then: While the ECG is set up, Ms. Villar points at the venous line: the blood is translucent, port-wine red.

choices.text: Give something for the pain and nausea and recheck in 20 minutes.
choices.feedback: Treating symptoms without a cause leaves the circuit running. If the blood is breaking down, every pass adds more potassium and free hemoglobin.
choices.then: Ten minutes later Ms. Villar calls you back. The blood in his line is translucent, port-wine red, and he is in more pain.

n2.scene: Ms. Villar asks whether to end the treatment and run saline to return his blood, as she would at the end of any session.

choices.text: Stop the blood pump and clamp the lines. Do not return the blood.
choices.feedback: Blood damaged in the circuit carries potassium released from broken red cells. Returning it can push the potassium dangerously high. In suspected hemolysis the blood is not returned.

choices.text: Yes, end the session and return the blood so he does not lose it.
choices.feedback: This is the instinct the call card warns against. Returning hemolyzed blood gives him a potassium load and more free hemoglobin. The volume is not worth the risk.
choices.then: You stop her before the saline runs. The pump is stopped and the lines are clamped.

choices.text: Lower the blood flow and continue while you look for a kink.
choices.feedback: A kink can cause hemolysis, but you have already looked and found none. Continuing, even slowly, keeps exposing his blood to the cause.
choices.then: On a second look there is still no kink. The pump is stopped and the lines are clamped.

n3.scene: As you turn, the patient two chairs away vomits and says her stomach aches. A third patient across the room says her chest feels tight. A staff member is already reaching for a saline bag to end the second patient’s treatment.

choices.text: Say aloud to the charge nurse that this is a possible cluster event: stop treatments under the cluster protocol starting with patients who have symptoms, return no blood, and hold all new starts.
choices.feedback: Three patients with the same new symptoms in one half hour are a unit problem until proved otherwise. Naming it out loud gets the whole team acting on one plan. The patients with symptoms are stopped and clamped first, without blood return.

choices.text: Go to each patient in turn and decide at each chair.
choices.feedback: Treating three patients as three separate problems loses minutes and lets staff make different calls, like the saline bag already in hand.
choices.then: By the time you reach the second chair her blood has been half returned. You stop it and tell the charge nurse that this is a cluster event.

choices.text: Let the staff return the blood for the other two, since only Mr. Santos has abnormal-looking blood so far.
choices.feedback: The other patients share the same water and dialysis fluid. Their lines may not look as dark yet, but their blood can still be hemolyzed. In a possible cluster, no affected patient has blood returned.
choices.then: The charge nurse stops the return and starts the cluster protocol.

n4.scene: The three patients with symptoms are on monitors with oxygen as the protocol directs, and urgent potassium and hemoglobin samples have gone to the laboratory. The technician comes to you.
n4.prompt: What do you ask the technician to do?

choices.text: Test the treated water for chlorine and chloramine now, check the dialysis fluid conductivity and temperature, and bring the water system log.
choices.feedback: Chloramine is not removed by reverse osmosis. Units rely on carbon, and the tanks were changed yesterday. Too dilute or too hot dialysis fluid also breaks red cells. You need these answers before anyone is reconnected.
choices.then: The total chlorine reading from the water after the carbon is above the unit’s limit.

choices.text: Swap the three dialyzers and blood lines for a new lot, then reconnect.
choices.feedback: A faulty tubing lot can cause a cluster, so keeping the lot numbers matters. But changing the circuit does nothing if the water or dialysis fluid is the cause, and no one is reconnected until the cause is known.
choices.then: You keep the lines and ask for the water tests. The total chlorine after the carbon is above the unit’s limit.

choices.text: Flush the machines and the water loop with fresh water to clear it quickly.
choices.feedback: Flushing before testing destroys the evidence and can hide the cause. The water, dialysis fluid, lines, and dialyzers are kept and sampled for the investigation.
choices.then: The technician tests first. Total chlorine after the carbon is above the unit’s limit.

n5.scene: Mr. Santos’s potassium is back at 6.4 mmol/L, and his monitor shows tall T waves. All patients are off the machines.
n5.prompt: Whom do you call, and what does the unit keep?

choices.text: The Medical Director and each attending nephrologist; arrange urgent hospital care for the patients with symptoms; keep the lines, dialyzers, lot numbers, water log, and water and dialysis fluid samples.
choices.feedback: A water or dialysis fluid fault involves the whole unit, so the Medical Director decides when it may restart. Each patient’s nephrologist needs to know. Hemolysis can be followed by severe hyperkalemia, so the affected patients need emergency evaluation and may need dialysis again on a safe circuit.

choices.text: Each attending nephrologist, and restart the other nine once the carbon is changed.
choices.feedback: The nephrologists must know. But restarting is the Medical Director’s decision, made after the water has been retested, not after one fix.

choices.text: Mr. Santos’s nephrologist only, since he is the sickest, and discard the used lines.
choices.feedback: Every affected patient’s nephrologist and the Medical Director need to know. Discarding the lines throws away evidence the root cause analysis needs.

vitals.unit: Closed; Medical Director to decide restart

end.title: After the event
end.text: The three patients with symptoms go to the emergency department for repeat potassium and hemoglobin and treatment of hyperkalemia. The unit stays closed until the Medical Director approves a restart after the carbon is replaced and the water retested. You write the times, the symptoms, the color of the blood, that blood was not returned and why, the readings, the lot numbers, and whom you called.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Look at the line. Back, abdominal, or chest pain with a rising blood pressure on dialysis, and translucent port-wine blood, means hemolysis until proved otherwise.
  • Do not return the blood in suspected hemolysis. The broken cells release potassium.
  • Two or more patients with one new complaint is a cluster. Say it aloud, stop treatments under the protocol starting with those who have symptoms, and hold new starts.
  • Chloramine passes through reverse osmosis. Exhausted carbon is a known cause of hemolysis outbreaks. Test before you flush.
  • Call the Medical Director for any water or dialysis fluid fault, and keep everything for the root cause analysis.

See the lesson parts Hemolysis and Cluster events.
